answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The Lancaster House Agreement was signed on 21 December 1979; a ceasefire followed with guerrillas in assembly points monitored by the Commonwealth; exiled leaders and refugees returned; elections in February 1980 gave ZANU-PF 57 seats, and Mugabe formed a government before independence on 18 April.

stem: Explain the policy of reconciliation adopted in 1980.

points.description: Meaning: setting aside past wrongs and working together.
Aim: prevent revenge and end bitterness.
Aim: keep white skills and capital for the economy.
Example: broad cabinet with ZAPU and white ministers.
Example: civil servants kept; property protected; no revenge trials.
Example: integration of the armies into the Zimbabwe National Army.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Reconciliation meant setting aside the wrongs of the past so that former enemies could build the nation together. Its aims were to prevent revenge, end the bitterness of the war and keep the skills and capital of whites so that the economy kept working. Examples include a cabinet with ZAPU leaders such as Nkomo and two white ministers, keeping most civil servants in their posts, protecting property and holding no revenge trials, and integrating ZANLA, ZIPRA and the Rhodesian forces into one army.

hints: Give the meaning, the aims and examples.

stem: Explain **two** limits of the policy of reconciliation.

points.description: Identifies continuing land and wealth inequality.
Explains: property was protected, so whites kept most farmland and businesses.
Identifies breakdown between ZANU-PF and ZAPU.
Explains: Entumbane clashes, Nkomo's dismissal (1982) and the disturbances that followed.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Because property was protected, whites kept most commercial farmland and businesses, so the inequality created by colonial rule continued. Reconciliation also did not unite the two liberation movements: clashes at Entumbane and the dismissal of Nkomo in 1982 led to the disturbances in Matabeleland and the Midlands.

hints: Think about the economy and about relations between the parties.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a letter from a fictional white farmer near Marondera to relatives in England, May 1980 (invented for this question)

> We expected the worst after the results. Instead the new Prime Minister spoke of forgiving and building together, and the district officer came to tell us nothing would change on the farms. Several neighbours who had their bags packed have unpacked them. We are staying.

**Source B** — the memories of a fictional former ZANLA combatant from Chimanimani, recorded in 2010 (invented for this question)

> We came out of the assembly point with nothing. They said reconciliation, and we agreed, because the war had to end. But the farm where my father worked as a labourer still belonged to the same man. We forgave, but the land did not come back.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: According to Source A, how did white farmers react to the policy of reconciliation?

points.description: They were reassured / relieved.
Many decided to stay (unpacked their bags).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far do Sources A and B agree about the effects of reconciliation? Explain your answer.

points.description: Agree: both say things did not change on the farms / ownership stayed the same.
Agree: both accepted reconciliation (A stays; B agreed it was necessary).
Disagree: A sees this as good news; B sees it as a disappointment.
Conclusion: they agree on the facts but differ in their judgement.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How useful are Sources A and B for assessing the achievements and limits of reconciliation? Use both sources and your own knowledge.

points.description: A: written in 1980 by someone who benefited; shows reassurance and whites staying (achievement).
A: one district, one viewpoint; written privately so may be honest.
B: a combatant's view, recorded 30 years later; may be shaped by later land reform debates.
B shows a limit: land unchanged, demobilised fighters had little.
Own knowledge: Lancaster House protected property; economy grew; tensions with ZAPU.
Supported judgement: useful together, each showing one side.

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A, a private letter written in 1980 by a white farmer, is useful evidence of an achievement of reconciliation: whites were reassured and many decided to stay, which helped the economy to grow in 1980-81. But it shows only the view of those who benefited. Source B, from a former ZANLA combatant recorded in 2010, shows a limit: demobilised fighters received little and the land remained with the same owners, because the Lancaster House constitution protected property. Recorded thirty years later, it may be influenced by later debates about land reform. Neither source mentions the breakdown between ZANU-PF and ZAPU. Together they are very useful, because they show both the stability reconciliation achieved and the inequality it left.

parts.explanation: Weigh both sources with own knowledge.

hints: Think about how the writers' positions affected what they saw.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Reconciliation had important successes. There was no wave of revenge after the war, many white farmers and professionals stayed, and the economy grew strongly in 1980-81 as aid and investment arrived. Three hostile armies were integrated into the Zimbabwe National Army.

But it had serious limits. Because the Lancaster House constitution protected property, land and wealth remained largely in white hands. Reconciliation also failed to hold together the two liberation movements: after clashes at Entumbane and the dismissal of Nkomo in 1982, the disturbances in Matabeleland and the Midlands caused great suffering until the Unity Accord of 22 December 1987.

Overall reconciliation succeeded in its immediate aim of a peaceful transition between black and white, but it was much less successful in creating national unity or economic justice in the 1980s.

parts.explanation: Top level weighs successes and limits.

hints: In (b), judge success against the aims of the policy.
